newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl sees EMU in 1999, more German jobs in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Kohl sees EMU in 1999, more German jobs in 1998.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl told doubters on Monday he was sure Europe's single currency would start on time in 1999 and Germany's record unemployment would ease by early next year.

Would-be members of European economic and monetary union (EMU) would meet the stringent debt and deficit criteria for joining the new club, he told reporters in Bonn after returning from a 10-day tour of Asia and the Pacific.
Kohl also said German economic growth would be around 2.5 percent this year and stronger in 1998, which would help bring a turnaround in the current record unemployment.

The Finance Ministry unexpectedly raised its 1997 unemployment forecast at the weekend, adding 120,000 more jobless to the 4.1 million average that economists say tears a hole in its budget and makes it harder to qualify for EMU.
"The euro will come," Kohl said confidently before a leadership meeting of his Christian Democratic Union.
Kohl, whose goal is to halve unemployment by the year 2000, said last week in New Zealand that he saw no signs of a turnaround in the rising jobless trend this year.
He spoke after official figures showed unemployment rose in April to a seasonally adjusted 4.299 million, the highest level for that month since 1945.

But Kohl said on Monday he expected a turnaround in the monthly labour market figures late this year or early in 1998. He said his comments last week referred to the average figure for this year, which he said would not change.
Containing unemployment is a key factor in Germany's bid to cut state borrowing this year to qualify for EMU.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said on Monday that Germany's new jobless forecast had not changed his opinion about Bonn's ability to be in the first wave of countries using the euro.
"My conviction still holds that the Germans will meet the currency criteria," he said in Brussels.

A Finance Ministry spokesman declined to comment on another EMU-related report at the weekend predicting that a sharp shortfall in first quarter tax revenues would cause another budget headache for Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
The Sunday newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported that tax shortfalls to be announced in an official report on Thursday would blow a 20-billion mark ($12 billion) hole in Waigel's 1997 budget.

Waigel said in late April that the shortfall could be 10 billion marks because of falling revenues and rising unemployment but it would definitely not be as high as the 20 billion marks the opposition Social Democrats estimate.

Kohl's comments about the Maastricht criteria, which set a ceiling for budget deficits at three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and debt at 60 percent of GDP, followed more tough remarks by German central bankers and Bavarian leaders against any weakening of the criteria.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer reiterated on Saturday his call for strict and lasting adherence to the criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

Tietmeyer said the euro alone would not provide a solution to the various challenges ahead for global markets. "That is why the selection of suitable participants on the basis of convincing and sustainable fulfilment of the convergence criteria is so important," he said.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber on Sunday urged a delay in the euro in Germany if Bonn failed to meet the deficit target.

"If we fail to reach the 3.0 percent deficit level in 1997, then our position remains that the criteria will determine the timing and not vice-versa," he said. "In other words, I prefer a delay to a weak currency." ($ = 1.668 German Marks)
